_readme: Not a failure on its own, which is why it is a separate row rather than folded
into the health gauge: a step-down is CORRECT during a deploy, when a new
revision takes the Redis lock. What it must not be is FREQUENT.
Repeated step-downs mean two instances are fighting over the lock, and the
cost is not just churn: each hand-over drops the socket, and the incoming
holder buys a metered REST snapshot on connect. A flapping leader spends
Tiingo quota on an unobservable budget while producing gaps in the bar series
that look like a quiet market.
> 0 in 15 minutes is chosen so a single deploy hand-over does page once — and
that is accepted deliberately. A deploy is a known, human-initiated event; a
flap is not, and the two are indistinguishable from the count alone. One
expected notification per release is cheaper than a threshold high enough to
name: [{{env}}] tiingo-realtime — leader stepped down
message:
tiingo-realtime's leader stepped down.

Expected ONCE per deploy, when the new revision takes the Redis lock. Anything else is a flap, and a flap is expensive twice over: every hand-over drops the socket, and the incoming holder buys a metered Tiingo REST snapshot to catch up.

If this repeats without a deploy: the leader lock is fail-CLOSED (no Redis, no leader), so check Redis reachability first — an unreachable lock produces no leader at all rather than two. Then check whether two revisions are genuinely overlapping; Cloud Run keeps the old one alive briefly on a replace, which is exactly what the lock exists to arbitrate.

@{{notify}}
